newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim vows to speed financial reform.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim vows to speed financial reform.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam pledged on Tuesday to speed up financial reform to eliminate corruption in the financial sector exposed by the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co.
Kim said funadamental changes were needed to overcome the current difficulties of the economy.
"I will expedite financial restructuring to root out corruption in the financial sector," he said.
The aim is to sever corrupt links between politicians and businessmen and let market forces dictate the economy.
In a televised address on the fourth anniversary of his inauguration, Kim apologised for a scandal involving Hanbo Steel, failed flagship of South Korea's 14th biggest conglomererate.
The nation's second largest steelmaker managed to borrow five trillion won ($5.8 billion), about 20 times its net worth, before being declared insolvent on January 23.
Kim gave no details of how he proposed to shake up the inefficient banking sector, one of the weak links in the South Korean economy.
Fostering mergers and allowing private bank ownership are widely seen as inevitable steps to reform the inefficient system, analysts said.
Currently, bank ownership is diluted with non-government shareholders limited to a maximum four percent holding. Bank heads are appointed after approval by a state watchdog body.
Opposition parties have called the loans the biggest financial scandal in the nation's history. They accuse the government of peddling influence to pressure banks into offering loans.

A total of 18 heads of local banks have been placed in custody or forced to resign since President Kim took office in 1993 on an anti-corruption platform. Most were found to have received bribes from borrowers.
Prosecutors have indicted 10 people over the Hanbo scandal, including three bankers -- two former presidents of Korea First Bank, Hanbo's biggest creditor, and the former head of Cho Hung Bank.
Successive South Korean governments have used the country's banks to support their industrial policy.
Kim also apologised over the controversial passage of a new labour law that was rammed through parliament with no debate.

"I feel sorry for worrying the public while revising the labour law late last year," he said. After a wave of nationwide strikes Kim sent the labour law back to parliament in January for further debate.
He told the nation on Tuesday, however, that South Korea must take steps to end "the high cost and low efficiency structure" that eroded the country's competitiveness.
More than three weeks of industrial strife hit the country's exports in January, pushing the trade deficit to a monthly record $3.48 billion.
The Japanese yen's fall against the dollar also hammered exports. The yen's weakness makes Japanese products more competitive against South Korean goods in overseas markets.
Hanbo's failure and the labour strife have forced economists to revise downward their forecast for the economy. Some say this year's growth could be the lowest in many years.
